text: Two beds, one room, and a lung disease indifferent to which of them is right. At the start of the 1950s a People's Police officer and a young Protestant curate are put together in a private sanatorium because consumption, not the state, assigns the beds. What follows is talk, and Lothar Warneke gives it the conditions of talk: fixed hours, thin walls, bodies that tire before the argument does. The screenplay took a European award, which is the right honor for a film in which everything that happens is something someone has decided to say out loud. Hubertus's difficulty with his own desire is never handed over to the church or to the socialist state for a ruling; it stays with him, which is the harder arrangement.

A professor emeritus of Roman law, out of money, reaches for the one remedy his subject still supplies in full: he offers himself to a former student as a slave. Leopoldo Contreras has translated the classics for years and been paid as though translation were a hobby, and the apartment is already sold. What Jaime de Armiñán gets from that premise is not a gag but a contract - board and lodging on one side, a body and its obedience on the other - and the awkward business of two educated men agreeing terms no modern law will recognize. The comedy comes from the pupil's discomfort as much as the teacher's dignity, and the drama from how quickly an arrangement entered in irony begins issuing real instructions.

Nearly everything in this film arrives secondhand: what the survivors told their questioners, what the neighbors remembered, what the men responsible said once they were asked. Faktas takes a wartime massacre in a Lithuanian village - a hundred people and more, held in houses that were then set alight - and declines to stage it as an experience. Almantas Grikevičius assembles it instead, testimony against testimony, until the shape of the day emerges from accounts that do not entirely agree. Ninety-one minutes is short for that much sorting, and the compression tells: no scene is allowed to run on feeling alone. Made in Lithuanian in 1981, it carries the further fact of who was doing the asking, and in which language the answers were filed.

A film about the previous year's news, shot while nobody involved yet knew how the war would end. Benghazi, 1941: the city is under British occupation, and the Italians living in it - civilians, and one captain who appears to have gone over to the other side - carry on with the ordinary business of a place while noticing what the garrison does. Augusto Genina works close to the domestic, which is where a wartime picture made in Italy in 1942 finds its charge: the risk sits not on a front line but at a table, in a doorway, in the short delay before an answer. The deception the film cares most about is one man's, and it is the kind that requires him to be despised by the people he is protecting.

Three hours and sixteen minutes inside a nursing home on the edge of Paris, about the pace at which the care being argued over insists on being given. Marie-Lou Fontaine has brought in a method called Humanitude and her staff want no part of it; the dispute is practical before it is philosophical, a matter of how many minutes one resident may be given in the morning. Into that argument comes Mari Morisaki, a Japanese playwright who is ill and knows it. Ryusuke Hamaguchi lets scenes run the length a conversation actually takes, so the runtime is not scale but method: an institution's habits change at the speed institutions change. Whatever the two women make of the place is contested daily by people who also have to work there.

One man went to prison for refusing to fight; the other, a priest, for killing someone who did. The war has just ended, and a French jail holds them both. Claude Autant-Lara arranges the meeting and then does the least cinematic thing available to him: he lets it become conversation, two hours of obedience examined from either end - who is owed it, what it excuses, whether a uniform or a collar alters the sum. The film was made sixteen years after the events it describes, near enough that nobody watching had to be told what was being asked of them. Neither man is a straw figure. The objector pays for his position in every scene where he has to explain it, and the priest's faith is not made simple in order to lose.

Ten years of marriage, and she had felt nothing; then her husband dies and the question of what she wants belongs to her alone. Jörn Donner takes that turn plainly, without arranging a lesson around it, and gives ninety-two minutes to a woman running an experiment on her own life. The Pole she meets is the occasion, not the subject. The film's attention stays on her: on the revisions a person makes to a daily schedule once the schedule has stopped being a duty, on the distance between grief and relief when both are in the room at once. What she does with the discovery is treated as work, slowly conducted. The Venice acting prize it carries is not decoration, since nearly everything of consequence happens on one face, in company, while she works out what she thinks.

The court has given her one more chance, which is not the same as anyone believing her. Nina Kern is not yet thirty, divorced, and her three children have lived in a home for some time on account of a neglect the record calls willful - a word the film has to either accept or work against for ninety-three minutes. Herrmann Zschoche mostly works against it, by staying close enough to a woman's week to show what promises cost when they have to be kept on a timetable other people set: appointments, inspections, the sober version of an evening. Custody here is not a sentiment but a schedule, kept under review by people who write things down. The lead performance took a Silver Bear and needed to. Everything in the picture depends on watching a woman be assessed and declining to join in.

She will not belong to her husband, and the village has no words for that except the ones it keeps for women. Malva runs eighty-four minutes and admits to a simple shape: a wife, a fisherman, the men who come within reach, a triangle that tightens. What keeps it from being only that is the flatness of the setting against the size of the feeling - a provincial shore where everyone's business is visible, and a woman who conducts hers anyway. Volodymyr Braun films the restlessness as appetite rather than symptom, as a fact about her instead of a diagnosis. A Venice acting prize sits on its record, and the place it was earned is visible: the seconds before she answers a question she has been asked before.

Two methods of weeping on a stage are in competition, and the older one is hers. Déryné has built a career on the grand gesture, the kind that has to carry to the back of a large house, and the younger rival arriving from Vienna does something quieter with her own feelings that audiences have begun to prefer. Gyula Maár makes this a question of employment rather than aesthetics: what a fading actress can still be cast as, and what she is offered instead. There is a husband she left, a newly built manor in the country, and the idea, entertained seriously for a while, that a person can simply stop. Ninety-three minutes, mostly in rooms, with a central performance that has to be good in two registers at once.

Fifteen minutes late for her own birth, and a whole life gets organized around the discrepancy. Annelie's parents had timed her arrival for midnight on the last night of 1871 and were disappointed by a clock; from there the film moves through her years in jumps, returning each time to the small failure of arithmetic that opened them. It is a comedy that keeps a straight face and a chronicle that refuses the weight chronicles usually take on - ninety-two minutes for decades, which means most of a life happens between the scenes. Josef von Báky treats the joke as a structure rather than a punchline, so the recurring quarter-hour stops being funny somewhere in the middle and becomes the way everyone who knows the story looks at her.

One method available to an occupying army: hang a dead donkey in the village square and leave it there until somebody talks. An Israeli doctor cuts it down, not as politics but out of revulsion, and the gesture is enough to move him from one side of the arrangement to the other, since disobedience is the only category the situation keeps for it. Shimon Dotan sets this on the West Bank and holds the scale domestic - a village, a governor with a bad idea, a hermit who takes the doctor in and whose adopted son is with the fighters everyone is hunting. Ninety-five minutes, made in 1986 from inside the country doing the occupying, which puts a particular weight on every scene where an Israeli is offered hospitality.

Four strangers wake in an empty room and are told, by a voice, that they are numbers now. The film withholds the rest: how they got there, what the voice wants, why refusal is answered with current. Eighty-five minutes on one situation and one set is a discipline as much as a budget, since obedience has to stay interesting without the relief of a corridor or a window. Silvio Nacucchi keeps the cruelty administrative rather than gory, and the crucial rule is that punishment can be transferred, so one person's stubbornness is paid for by the person beside them. That transfer is the real subject: not the voice, which is only a machine for producing pressure, but four people learning what they will do to each other to make it stop.

Kieu is in love with Love itself, and the film treats that as a condition to be examined rather than a charm to be enjoyed. Trịnh T. Minh-hà builds a Vietnamese immigrant's story out of materials that keep announcing themselves: actors who never pretend to be unobserved, scenes that are plainly staged, remembered time laid over present time. Voyeurism is the through-line, and the film's own interest in a woman is placed on the table beside everyone else's. Once that is in the open, the ordinary pleasures of a romance become impossible to take innocently. A hundred and eight minutes built to be watched the way a book is read: attentive to the seams, willing to lose the thread and find it again elsewhere.
